plants.name: Colchicum autumnale
plants.description: Just as the garden begins to fade, chalice-shaped blooms of soft lilac-pink and white rise straight from bare soil. They have no leaves, as if they were conjured overnight. Clusters of them carpet lawns and borders with a delicate late-season glow.
plants.location: Central and Western Europe, and gardens across the temperate Northern Hemisphere, including the US Midwest
plants.funFact: The leaves appear in spring and die back by summer. The flowers then emerge alone in autumn, which earns the plant the nickname 'naked ladies'. Every part of it is highly toxic.

plants.name: Protea cynaroides
plants.description: South Africa's national flower is a spectacular bloom up to 30 cm across. A crown of silky, blush-pink bracts surrounds a central cone of tiny flowers. It stands out against the fynbos shrubland of the Cape.
plants.bloomingSeason: Mainly June to October, peaking in the Southern Hemisphere's late winter and spring
plants.location: Fynbos of the Western and Eastern Cape, South Africa
plants.funFact: The 'flower' is actually a cluster of many small flowers in a head, surrounded by showy bracts. The plant belongs to an ancient family that dates back to the age of Gondwana.

plants.name: Acacia pycnantha
plants.description: Branches become heavy with fluffy, fragrant golden pom-poms that light up the Australian bush in the closing weeks of winter. Each ball is a burst of dozens of tiny flowers, and they draw bees and birds in large numbers.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late August to September (late winter to early spring)
plants.location: Southeastern Australia, including Victoria, South Australia and New South Wales
plants.funFact: Golden wattle is Australia's national floral emblem. Each golden ball is made up of 40 to 80 tiny flowers, and the country celebrates it every 1 September on Wattle Day.
